props.title: A Close Shave
props.initialSlug: Wallace & Gromit battle sheep-rustling robot menace

sections.content: A Close Shave (1995) represents Aardman Animation's pinnacle of stop-motion craftsmanship before their breakthrough feature Chicken Run (2000). This third Wallace & Gromit adventure amplifies everything that made The Wrong Trousers (1993) brilliant - the noir atmosphere, ingenious gadgets, and perfectly-timed sight gags. Nick Park's 30-minute masterpiece introduces both the villainous Preston and Shaun the Sheep, who later spawned his own massively successful franchise. The film's wool-shortage mystery plays like Hitchcock by way of Toy Story (1995), mixing genuine suspense with impeccable comic timing.

sections.content: The mid-90s marked a renaissance for stop-motion animation. While Toy Story (1995) was revolutionizing CGI, artists like Nick Park and Henry Selick were pushing practical animation to new heights. The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993) proved stop-motion could sustain feature length, while James and the Giant Peach (1996) seamlessly blended it with live action. A Close Shave stands as a bridge between animation's practical past and digital future, maintaining the handcrafted charm that CGI often struggles to replicate. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation in Stop-Motion

The sophistication of A Close Shave's animation is staggering. The motorcycle chase sequence required unprecedented mechanical precision, with Wallace and Gromit's bike splitting apart and reassembling in real-time. This influenced later stop-motion achievements like Coraline (2009) and Kubo and the Two Strings (2016). The film's blend of comedy and suspense also inspired ParaNorman (2012) and The Boxtrolls (2014), proving character-driven stop-motion could rival any animation medium.
